newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: High crude prices seen biting S.Korean economy.
newsitem.headline: High crude prices seen biting S.Korean economy.

text.p: High crude oil prices are expected to deal a heavy blow to South Korea by deepening a snowballing trade deficit and spiraling inflation, economists and analysts said on Wednesday.

"This is definitely bad news for Korea," said Kim Sung-shik, senior economist at the private LG Economic Research Institute. "Strong crude prices would play a negative role on the already huge trade deficit."

The benchmark North Sea Brent rose to a post-Gulf War high of $24.39 on September 12, days after the United States had launched a series of missile attacks on Iraq. It has since fallen to $21.85 on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) on Wednesday.
Brent prompt month futures prices are almost 10 percent higher in the year to the end of August compared with the 1995 average price.
South Korea, which produces no crude oil, depends wholly on imports. Crude imports take up over eight percent of the nation's total imports, 12.4 percent when oil products are included.

The nation's trade deficit ballooned to $11.6 billion in the first seven months of the year against $6.5 billion a year earlier. The shortfall is mainly the result of plunging prices for semiconductors, steel and petrochemical products, South Korea's major export items.
"South Korea is likely to end up the biggest victim in Asia of strong oil prices," said Shin Hoo-shik, a senior economist at the private Daewoo Economic Research Institute.
He said Japan is structurally geared more towards energy conservation, while Taiwan's relatively favourable weather conditions help energy savings.

A rise in crude prices is also seen fuelling South Korea's inflation as the government will inevitably have to raise the domestic price of oil products next month to reflect strong crude and product prices.
Local oil product prices are set on the first day of each month based on the previous month's global crude oil prices and Singapore spot quotes.
Kim of LG said the government may attempt to soften the impact on domestic oil prices by reducing the government tax on the products.
"The government will try to lessen the impact on consumer prices," he said. "But a rise in local petroleum product prices will be unpreventable."

The consumer price index rose 5.3 percent in August on the year, up from a 3.5 percent rise a year earlier. For the first eight months of this year, the index gained 4.4 percent, just slightly off the year's 4.5 percent target.
Although curbing the rising inflation and narrowing the trade deficit have been the top priority of Seoul's economic policy, there's not much the policy makers can do, economists said.

"We do expect some pressure on the trade deficit, but we haven't prepared any countermeasures," said a senior official at the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, who asked not to be named. "We anticipate the tension in the Middle East to be temporary."
